tagline: A country built below the sea
overview:
The Netherlands is a small, flat, crowded country on the North Sea coast of Western Europe, sharing borders with Germany and Belgium. About a quarter of its land lies below sea level, held back by dunes, dikes, and enormous storm barriers; much of that land was once seabed, pumped dry over centuries to make fields called polders. All together it is roughly twice the size of New Jersey.

About 18 million people live here and speak Dutch, and nearly everyone learns English at school as well. Amsterdam, laced with canals and tall narrow houses, is the capital, while the king, government, and parliament sit in The Hague, which also hosts international courts. The Netherlands is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament and was a founding member of the European Union.

Bicycles outnumber people, trains link compact cities, and fields and glass greenhouses make this small country one of the world's biggest exporters of food.
landAndNature: The Netherlands is famously level: its highest point, the Vaalserberg in the far southeast, reaches only 322 meters, and much of the country is a patchwork of drained polders divided by straight canals and ditches. The Rhine, Meuse, and Scheldt rivers meet here in a wide delta before spilling into the North Sea, and the Delta Works, a system of dams, sluices, and movable barriers, guards the southwest against storm surges. Along the north coast the Wadden Sea drains twice a day into vast mudflats where seals rest and millions of migrating birds feed. Spring brings tulip fields in stripes of color, and storks, spoonbills, and godwits nest in the wet meadows.
peopleAndCulture: Dutch life is organized around bicycles: there are more bikes than people, and children ride to school in all weather on separate red-paved paths. People have a reputation for being direct, punctual, and fond of gezelligheid, a hard-to-translate word for cozy togetherness. The food is plain and good: herring eaten with raw onion, stroopwafels, thin pancakes, cheeses such as Gouda and Edam, and salty licorice. Dutch painters changed art forever, from Rembrandt and Vermeer to Van Gogh. Soccer is the national game, and the Dutch style called Total Football reshaped the sport in the 1970s. Speed skating is huge, and when the canals freeze hard, whole towns take to the ice.
history: Germanic and Celtic tribes lived in this delta when Rome reached the Rhine. In the Middle Ages trading towns grew rich on shipping and wool, and in 1568 the Dutch provinces rebelled against Spanish rule, winning independence after eighty years of war. The 1600s were the Dutch Golden Age: Amsterdam became Europe's richest port and home to the world's first stock exchange, while the Dutch East and West India Companies built a trading empire from Indonesia to the Caribbean and New York, seizing colonies and trafficking hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Nazi Germany occupied the country from 1940 to 1945 and murdered about 100,000 Dutch Jews, among them Anne Frank. After the war the Netherlands helped found the European Union.
funFacts: Dutch people are the tallest in the world on average, with men close to 1.83 meters.
Schiphol Airport near Amsterdam sits about four meters below sea level, on the bed of a lake that was drained in the 1850s.
Kinderdijk has nineteen windmills from the 1700s that once pumped water out of the polders using wind power alone.
Nearly all Dutch children earn a swimming diploma, practicing in clothes and shoes, because water is never far away.
King's Day on April 27 turns the whole country orange, and children sell their old toys on the sidewalks.
